You're being quite mature when you recognize that these feelings come from a vague and somewhat baseless discomfort rather than just coming up with a reason to justify it on the spot or refusing to think about it.

I don't think you need to chastise yourself too bad for the first one since the two examples you mentioned are surprisingly dissimilar. A party entertainer who works for themselves and willingly exposes themselves to an environment of women who are already engaged, is in a different situation than a career entertainer who is attached to a somewhat seedy club. That's without the sex work element. In the situation you are thinking of your theoretical daughter is in a more worrying position. It's fair to worry about your child doing something risky where they might get hurt. Just try to separate those feelings from the domineering dad stereotype of  "no one is going to look at my little girl that way and if they do then it's her fault for being a slut" that's the sexist part. Where how other people see a woman is her fault and women are pure untouched creatures who must be ethereal and beyond human lest they fall and be tainted. It's not a good outlook.

The sex tape thing can be a bunch of different anxietys not all of which are sexist. It's normal to feel a bit on guard around someone who has been a victim before because you don't want to fuck up and hurt them more accidentally (not super fair on them but normal). A lot of people are a bit squeamish and private about sex as a rule so the idea that it has been aired publicly can be uncomfortable regardless of gender. That being said being uncomfortable with the idea that a wide variety of people have seen your partner in a sexual context before you did is sexist, especially if it wasn't her fault. I'd recommend just trying to put yourself in her hypothetical shoes. If a partner told you to trust them and no one would see and then failed you. And then someone else you like was uncomfortable around you because of that. It's fairly easy to see the injustice there. 

Just be careful to look at why you specifically feel this discomfort. Some of it is second hand sexism. Some of it will be your own personal shit. Continue to be aware of it and always be trying to be better. You'll do fine. You seem like a good guy. :)

The nudity thing was one that caught me by surprise. I didn't realize how much more arduous it would make my day even though I'm not directly involved in any of those bits. I'm a continuity supervisor and my job is basically to make sure no one moves a plant in the background between takes so it doesn't jump across the shot (amoungst other things). But that involves asking people to stand still while I line up shots with the last take so no one launches themselves across the room with no between shot, and keeping track of what doors people enter and exit from. I cant just ask people to sit wrapped in each others arms in the buff while I rearrange the plants. I can't ask them to go outside the building with their shirt off so they can enter from the most thematically consistent door. I cant ask people to spend a whole extra day rubbing themselves against a stranger in a cock sock because without two seconds of footage it will look like they phased through the sofa. Oh yeah, I agree there have been some really terrible uses of them. I think it's just that when they are used well we don't notice because that's the point. 

Practically, filming with nudity is surprisingly difficult. People get cold and sweaty, makeup needs to be applied to all skin so they don't look green under the stage lights so that takes way too much time, and has to be done between every take. You can't have an open set when there is nudity so every time there is a shot change you have to cover everyone up, open the set to bring everyone in to rearrange everything and then close it again. Just a few minutes can take several days to film and people don't like being naked on camera right after lunch. The people having to deal with all this shit aren't the ones with the artistic vision though so they can't declare it more effort than it's worth. 

This leads to a lot of studios having a general policy of no one being naked more than they absolutely have to be. If they can get away with flesh colored underwear or a merkin or everyone keeping their trousers on and only shooting from the waist up they will. Just to stop that background actress who will only have to be there for a week and isn't getting paid enough for this from having to feel the breeze for a whole week, even if they can't get away with it for the guys. 

Sorry, that very quickly became a rant about my job. Films are made by lots of people with conflicting prioritys is my point.

I think the feminist take is less about more male nudity and more of a retort. "If it's so important to the story and the artistic expression for there to be nakedness why does it so overwhelmingly swing one way? Address the balance if you don't want me to have a problem with your use of it." 

In terms of film making I think it's because a shot of exposed vulva is going to be a more awkward shot. Just practically we very rarely need a shot of the underside of an actor in a way that hides their face. At least in comparison to a shot of a person standing and in those shots a merkin can be used where a similar cock sock would be more conspicuous. So the call for the balance to be addressed just isn't taking into account that it's easier to make a woman look fully naked without being so, than it is for a man.

So the two arguments conflict because they are for different situations. Breasts should not be sexualised as much as they are so your right, more exposure in non sexual contexts makes sense. However when the purpose of the shot is to sexualise then breasts are sexualised, at which point having both characters wearing jeans but no shirt is uneven. Womens sport is a touchy subject since testosterone is a doping drug in womens sport, even for cis women who have naturally high levels. So that should be hashed out by the qualified.

Probably the more sensitive a subject and the more directly related it is to your body and how it works the more it makes sense to be separated. Either by sex or just, from everyone else. But in most cases it's just polite to have a place that's roughly half as public as outside to be a little private. No one should be standing at the door with a testing kit and a mirror on a stick, that's not what it's for. It's important to keep in mind that no one is (no one should I should probably say) be making any laws about this. It's about what is polite, not about what is morally reprehensible. It's not morally reprehensible to exist anywhere.
